e-6633.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
t^2 y'' - 4ty' + 6y = 2t+6, \quad t > 0
$$

has the complementary solution $y_c(t) =  At^3 + Bt^2,$ find the particular solution $y_p(t)$ to this equation.
e-6633.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $2t+6.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
y_p(t) = \alpha t + \beta
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p$ gives

$$
y_p' =  \alpha,
\qquad y_p'' = 0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}(0)-4t(\alpha )+6(\alpha t+\beta ) & =2t+6 \\ (-4\alpha +6\alpha )t+6\beta  & =2t+6 \\ 2\alpha t+6\beta  & =2t+6\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,t) \\ 6\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular solution $y_p(t)$ is

$$
y_p(t) = t + 1.
$$

Question 2
?

Given that the differential equation

t2y″+2ty′=12t3−24t2,t>0

has the complimentary function yc(t)=A+Bt, find the particular solution yp(t) to this equation.

a
yp(t)=4t3+6t2
b
yp(t)=−6t3−t2
c
yp(t)=t3−4t2
d
yp(t)=−t3+5t
e
yp(t)=2t3−3t
Submit

decision.explanation: Try y_p(t)=αt^3+βt^2. Then t^2y_p''+2ty_p'=12αt^3+6βt^2. Matching 12t^3-24t^2 gives α=1 and β=-4, so option c satisfies the equation.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+2t{y}^{′}=12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2},\,t>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(t)=A+\frac{B}{t}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ to this equation.
after.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2}.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha {t}^{3}+\beta {t}^{2},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=3\alpha {t}^{2}+2\beta t,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=6\alpha t+2\beta .
$$

 

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}(6\alpha t+2\beta )+2t(3\alpha {t}^{2}+2\beta t) & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2} \\ (6\alpha +6\alpha ){t}^{3}+(2\beta +4\beta ){t}^{2} & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2} \\ 12\alpha {t}^{3}+6\beta {t}^{2} & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}12\alpha =12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{t}^{3}) \\ 6\beta =-24\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{t}^{2})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1,\,\,\beta =-4.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)={t}^{3}-4{t}^{2}.
$$

content.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+2t{y}^{′}=12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2},\,t>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(t)=A+\frac{B}{t}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ to this equation.
content.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2}.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha {t}^{3}+\beta {t}^{2},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=3\alpha {t}^{2}+2\beta t,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=6\alpha t+2\beta .
$$

 

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}(6\alpha t+2\beta )+2t(3\alpha {t}^{2}+2\beta t) & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2} \\ (6\alpha +6\alpha ){t}^{3}+(2\beta +4\beta ){t}^{2} & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2} \\ 12\alpha {t}^{3}+6\beta {t}^{2} & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}12\alpha =12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{t}^{3}) \\ 6\beta =-24\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{t}^{2})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1,\,\,\beta =-4.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)={t}^{3}-4{t}^{2}.
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
4{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+2x{y}^{′}-6y=2x-3,\,x>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)=\frac{A}{x}+Bx\sqrt{x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
after.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is  $2x-3.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta ,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}\cdot 0+2x(\alpha )-6(\alpha x+\beta ) & =2x-3 \\ (2\alpha -6\alpha )x-6\beta  & =2x-3 \\ -4\alpha x-6\beta  & =2x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ -6\beta =-3\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2},\,\,\beta =\frac{1}{2}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.
$$

a
yp(x)=x212−112
b

decision.explanation: Let y_p(x)=αx²+β. Then y_p'=2αx and y_p''=2α, so substitution gives -6αx²-12β=2x²+1. Matching coefficients yields α=-1/3 and β=-1/12, proving option b.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+2x{y}^{′}-12y=2{x}^{2}+1,\,x>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{x}^{3}+\frac{B}{{x}^{4}}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
after.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is  $2{x}^{2}+1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta ,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(2\alpha )+2x(2\alpha x)-12(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta ) & =2{x}^{2}+1 \\ (2\alpha +4\alpha -12\alpha ){x}^{2}-12\beta  & =2{x}^{2}+1 \\ -6\alpha {x}^{2}-12\beta  & =2{x}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ -12\beta =1\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{3},\,\,\beta =-\frac{1}{12}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{12}.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Particular Solution For a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Forcing
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+2x{y}^{′}-12y=2{x}^{2}+1,\,x>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{x}^{3}+\frac{B}{{x}^{4}}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
content.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is  $2{x}^{2}+1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta ,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(2\alpha )+2x(2\alpha x)-12(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta ) & =2{x}^{2}+1 \\ (2\alpha +4\alpha -12\alpha ){x}^{2}-12\beta  & =2{x}^{2}+1 \\ -6\alpha {x}^{2}-12\beta  & =2{x}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ -12\beta =1\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{3},\,\,\beta =-\frac{1}{12}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{12}.
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-4x{y}^{′}+6y=-6x+1,\,x>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{x}^{2}+B{x}^{3}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
after.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $-6x+1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta ,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(0)-4x(\alpha )+6(\alpha x+\beta ) & =-6x+1 \\ (-4\alpha +6\alpha )x+6\beta  & =-6x+1 \\ 2\alpha x+6\beta  & =-6x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =-6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 6\beta =1\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-3$ and $\beta =\frac{1}{6}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$

content.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-4x{y}^{′}+6y=-6x+1,\,x>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{x}^{2}+B{x}^{3}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
content.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $-6x+1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta ,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(0)-4x(\alpha )+6(\alpha x+\beta ) & =-6x+1 \\ (-4\alpha +6\alpha )x+6\beta  & =-6x+1 \\ 2\alpha x+6\beta  & =-6x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =-6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 6\beta =1\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-3$ and $\beta =\frac{1}{6}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-3x+\frac{1}{6}.
$$
